name: open() and the three modes
desc: "w" writes and WIPES whatever was there. "a" adds to the end. "r" reads. Choose carefully.
code:
f = open("notes.txt", "w")
f.write("first line\n")
f.write("second line\n")
f.close()

f = open("notes.txt", "r")
print(f.read())
f.close()

name: "w" wipes the file
desc: The mistake that loses work. Opening in w mode empties the file before you write a single thing.
code:
open("data.txt", "w").write("original content\n")

open("data.txt", "w").write("new content\n")   # the original is GONE

print(open("data.txt").read())

name: "a" adds instead
desc: Append mode keeps what is already there and writes underneath it.
code:
open("log.txt", "w").write("line 1\n")
open("log.txt", "a").write("line 2\n")
open("log.txt", "a").write("line 3\n")

print(open("log.txt").read())

name: read / readline / readlines
desc: read gives one big string, readline gives one line, readlines gives a list of lines.
code:
open("f.txt", "w").write("alpha\nbeta\ngamma\n")

f = open("f.txt")
print(repr(f.readline()))
f.close()

f = open("f.txt")
print(f.readlines())
f.close()

name: Looping over a file
desc: The normal way to read a file line by line. strip() takes the newline off each one.
code:
open("f.txt", "w").write("HR\nTech\nSales\n")

f = open("f.txt")
for line in f:
    print("[" + line.strip() + "]")
f.close()

name: with open()  —  closes it for you
desc: The version to actually use. The file is closed automatically, even if the code inside fails.
code:
with open("f.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("written safely\n")

with open("f.txt") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())

print("file closed?", f.closed)

name: Why it exists
desc: Without it, one bad value stops the whole program and nothing after it runs.
out:
10
20
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'

name: try  /  except
desc: Try the risky line. If it fails, run the except block instead of stopping.
out:
10
20
abc is not a number - skipped
30

name: Catching a SPECIFIC error
desc: A bare except hides every problem, including the ones you wanted to know about. Name the error.

name: More than one except
desc: Different problems, different handling. Python runs the first one that matches.
out:
5.0
not a number: abc
divisor was zero

name: else  and  finally
desc: else runs only when nothing failed. finally runs either way — it is where you clean up.

name: The error names worth knowing
desc: Each one tells you something different. Read the name before you read anything else.
out:
ValueError - invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
ZeroDivisionError - division by zero
IndexError - list index out of range
KeyError - 'b'
TypeError - can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

name: class and object
desc: A class is the blueprint. An object is one real thing built from it. One class, many objects.
code:
class Employee:
    pass

e1 = Employee()
e2 = Employee()
print(type(e1))
print(e1 is e2)      # two different objects

name: __init__  and  self
desc: __init__ runs automatically when an object is made. self is that object — it is how each one keeps its own values.
code:
class Employee:
    def __init__(self, name, dept, salary):
        self.name = name
        self.dept = dept
        self.salary = salary

e = Employee("Rahul", "HR", 47764)
print(e.name, e.dept, e.salary)

name: Methods
desc: A function inside a class. It always takes self first, so it can reach the object's own values.

name: Each object keeps its own data
desc: This is the point of self. Two objects from one class do not share anything.
code:
class Employee:
    def __init__(self, name, salary):
        self.name = name
        self.salary = salary

a = Employee("Rahul", 47764)
b = Employee("Priya", 62990)

a.salary = 50000
print(a.name, a.salary)
print(b.name, b.salary)     # untouched

name: Objects in a list
desc: Once objects are in a list you can loop over them like any other data. This is where it becomes useful.
code:
class Employee:
    def __init__(self, name, dept, salary):
        self.name, self.dept, self.salary = name, dept, salary

staff = [Employee("Rahul", "HR", 47764),
         Employee("Priya", "Tech", 62990),
         Employee("Amit", "Sales", 51200)]

for e in staff:
    print(e.name.ljust(8), e.dept.ljust(7), e.salary)

total = sum(e.salary for e in staff)
print("total payroll:", total)
print("average      :", total / len(staff))
out:
Rahul    HR      47764
Priya    Tech    62990
Amit     Sales   51200
total payroll: 161954
average      : 53984.666666666664

name: Filtering a list of objects
desc: Everything you learned about lists still applies — the items just happen to be objects.

name: The four, in one line each
desc: Introduced together in the last session. Each one is a way of organising code, not a new syntax.
code:
print("ENCAPSULATION  keep the data and the code that uses it together")
print("INHERITANCE    a class can take everything another class has")
print("POLYMORPHISM   the same method name behaving differently")
print("ABSTRACTION    show what it does, hide how it does it")
out:
ENCAPSULATION  keep the data and the code that uses it together
INHERITANCE    a class can take everything another class has
POLYMORPHISM   the same method name behaving differently
ABSTRACTION    show what it does, hide how it does it

name: Encapsulation
desc: The data and the methods that work on it live in the same class. Two underscores marks something as internal.

name: Inheritance
desc: Put the parent class in the brackets and the child gets everything it has, for free.

name: super()  —  extending the parent
desc: Call the parent's version first, then add to it, instead of rewriting what already works.

name: Polymorphism  —  overriding
desc: The child defines a method the parent already has. Same name, different behaviour.
out:
does the work
assigns the work
does the work

name: Abstraction
desc: The caller uses hike() without knowing how it works. A base class can name a method and leave the detail to the children.
